policy.purpose: Core (1A) is the difficulty-aware, prior-knowledge-aware subtopic-bucket teaching layer between source/Core (1) semantics and Core (2) transfer.
policy.primary_question_rule: Each Revised Core (2) v2 question belongs to exactly one primary SBA bucket; secondary prerequisites may be attached separately.
policy.production_selection_rule: For the current build queue, do not publish a dedicated SBA PDF when core2_primary_questions is empty; retain the bucket in the chapter map as SKIP_NO_PRIMARY_CORE2.
policy.priority_rule: Prioritise MEDIUM/HARD buckets for learners at or below 50% usable prior knowledge; increase visual staging, prerequisite rebuilding and worked-example guidance as readiness falls.
policy.core2_hint_preteach_rule: Every Core (2) H1/H2/H3 reveal must trace to an earlier Core (1A) learning atom and to an example/check; a question may be held until its release prerequisite buckets are complete.
policy.teaching_sequence_rule: Foundation/pretraining -> story/phenomenon -> staged picture -> what changed physically -> picture-to-maths bridge -> worked example -> guided/faded practice -> retrieval gate -> Core (2).

buckets.production_reason: Has one or more primary Revised Core (2) v2 questions; publish according to difficulty/readiness.

learning_atoms.title: The same-height model contract
learning_atoms.purpose: Separate the special launch-and-landing-at-the-same-height model from tower or unequal-height projectile problems before using T, R or H shortcuts.
teaching_moves: draw a launch and landing point on the same horizontal line
contrast with a tower/unequal-height landing
state the ideal-model conditions
name T, R and H as conditional same-height tools
misconceptions: same-height formulas work for every projectile
range always means horizontal distance until y becomes zero in any coordinate setup
checks: classify a sketch as same-height or unequal-height before choosing formulas

learning_atoms.title: Time of flight comes from vertical symmetry
learning_atoms.purpose: Build total flight time from the vertical component and the apex condition rather than memorising T in isolation.
teaching_moves: show ascent and descent sharing one vertical story
use v_y=0 at the apex to get t_up=u_y/g
use same-height symmetry to double ascent time
substitute u_y=u sin(theta)
misconceptions: horizontal speed decides the flight time
same-height symmetry means velocity is identical on both sides
checks: connect equal flight time to equal initial vertical components

learning_atoms.title: Maximum height and inverse vertical-component use
learning_atoms.purpose: Derive maximum height from the vertical no-time relation and run the relation backwards when H is given.
teaching_moves: mark the apex as v_y=0
apply v_y^2=u_y^2-2gH
solve H=u_y^2/(2g)
substitute u_y=u sin(theta)
reverse the relation to u_y=sqrt(2gH) when height is given
misconceptions: maximum height is measured from ground regardless of origin
height determines the whole launch speed instead of the vertical component
checks: recover u_y from a given H
then obtain T from the recovered vertical component

learning_atoms.title: Range is horizontal speed times total flight time
learning_atoms.purpose: Derive the same-height range formula by combining constant horizontal velocity with the vertical flight time.
teaching_moves: show horizontal spacing continuing through the entire shared flight time
write R=u_x T
substitute u_x=u cos(theta) and T=2u sin(theta)/g
use 2sin(theta)cos(theta)=sin(2theta)
misconceptions: range is produced by a new horizontal force
R=u^2 sin(2theta)/g can be used when landing height differs
checks: rebuild the range formula from u_x and T
state its validity condition before use

learning_atoms.title: Maximum range and range scaling with angle
learning_atoms.purpose: Show that at fixed speed only sin(2theta) controls same-height range and use that factor for maximum-range and scaling questions.
teaching_moves: separate the fixed factor u^2/g from the angle factor sin(2theta)
compare angle-factor values visually
identify the maximum sin(2theta)=1 at theta=45 degrees
connect R_max=u^2/g and u_x=u_y=u/sqrt(2)
use proportional reasoning before full calculation
misconceptions: larger launch angle always gives larger range
checks: identify 45 degrees as the maximum-range angle
scale range when only the angle changes
recover u and a component from a given maximum range

learning_atoms.title: Complementary angles give equal range
learning_atoms.purpose: Explain why theta and 90 degrees-theta have equal range at the same speed while their times and heights differ.
teaching_moves: draw a low and a high trajectory with the same endpoints
compare sin(2theta) and sin(180 degrees-2theta)
show equal range
contrast vertical components, flight times and heights
misconceptions: complementary shots have equal flight time and height
checks: predict which complementary shot stays longer in air
state which quantity is guaranteed equal

learning_atoms.title: Compare time and height using angle ratios
learning_atoms.purpose: Use proportional forms T proportional to sin(theta) and H proportional to sin^2(theta) for fixed speed without carrying unnecessary common factors.
teaching_moves: factor out the common 2u/g in T comparisons
factor out the common u^2/(2g) in H comparisons
compare 30 and 60 degree sines
square only for height ratios
misconceptions: forget to square the sine for height

learning_atoms.title: Complementary-height pair and angle convention
learning_atoms.purpose: Connect complementary launch angles to H_1=K sin^2(theta), H_2=K cos^2(theta), and handle questions where an angle is measured from the vertical.
teaching_moves: define K=u^2/(2g)
write the two complementary heights as K sin^2(theta) and K cos^2(theta)
use sin^2+cos^2=1 to obtain H_1+H_2=K
translate an angle measured from vertical before choosing sine/cosine
equate vertical components for equal flight time
misconceptions: treat an angle from vertical as if measured from horizontal
equal flight time requires equal launch speed rather than equal vertical component
checks: translate a vertical-referenced angle to the correct vertical component

learning_atoms.title: Range-height ratio removes unnecessary unknowns
learning_atoms.purpose: Derive R/H=4cot(theta) and use it as a direct bridge for range-height questions, including the remaining same-height step needed by Q14 and Q27.
teaching_moves: divide the range and maximum-height formulas
cancel u^2/g before substituting numbers
simplify to 4cot(theta)
work R=H as tan(theta)=4
use the ratio after reconstructing launch components when required
misconceptions: solve R and H separately when their ratio cancels common unknowns
forget that the ratio relation assumes same-height flight
checks: solve a direct R/H angle problem
release Q14 and Q27 after adding the same-height relation they require

hint_rungs.evidence: Maximum height is explicitly tied to the initial vertical component.
H=u_y^2/(2g) is paired with T=2u_y/g and worked in both directions.
Guided inverse example starts by writing u_y=sqrt(2gH).
Maximum range is identified as the 45 degree same-height case.
R_max=u^2/g is derived from the angle factor.
Worked practice begins by setting the given maximum range equal to u^2/g.
Equal total flight time is connected to equal initial vertical components.
Angles measured from vertical are translated before resolving the vertical component.
Guided comparison equates the two u_y values first.
Maximum horizontal distance is tied to theta=45 degrees.
R_max=u^2/g and u_x=u/sqrt(2) are taught together.
Worked bridge first recovers u^2 from the given maximum range.
Same speed plus equal range is connected to complementary launch angles.
Complementary heights are represented as K sin^2(theta) and K cos^2(theta).
The first move is to use H_1+H_2=K before solving for the angle.
For fixed u, flight time is shown proportional to sin(theta).
30 degree and 60 degree sine factors are compared without unnecessary constants.
Guided ratio starts with T_30:T_60=sin30:sin60.
For fixed u, maximum height is shown proportional to sin^2(theta).
30 degree and 60 degree squared-sine factors are compared.
Guided ratio starts with H_30:H_60=sin^2(30):sin^2(60).
30 degrees and 60 degrees are identified as a complementary pair.
Equal range is represented using the sin(2theta) symmetry.
The comparison explicitly uses sin60 degrees and sin120 degrees.
The same-height model is recognized before applying a time shortcut.
T=2u sin(theta)/g is derived rather than listed alone.
Worked example begins by inserting the given u and theta into the time relation.
The learner is taught to prefer R/H when the ratio is given.
R/H=4cot(theta) is derived from the two source formulas.
Guided example starts by equating 4cot(theta) to the stated ratio.
With speed fixed, only the sin(2theta) factor changes the range.
Range scaling is represented through relative sin(2theta) factors.
The worked bridge sets the target factor to 1 before solving 2theta=90 degrees.
Range-height ratio is identified as the shortest route.
A direct 4cot(theta) relation is available without solving R and H separately.
Guided practice isolates cot(theta) as the first algebraic move.
Complementary 30 degree and 60 degree shots are shown to have equal range but different heights.
Height comparison uses H proportional to sin^2(theta).
The guided comparison starts with sin^2(60):sin^2(30).
